newsitem.title: USA: Killer's head catches fire in botched U.S. execution. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Killer's head catches fire in botched U.S. execution. [CORRECTED 17:00 GMT]

text.p: Flame and smoke shot from a convicted killer's head when Florida's electric chair malfunctioned during a botched execution on Tuesday.
A six-inch (15 cm) flame and cloud of smoke shot from the head of a convicted killer Pedro Medina as he died, prison officials said.
(Corrects metric conversion in above paragraph from 67 cm.)

Despite the fire and smoke, prisons spokeswoman Kerry Slack said the execution was not interrupted and Medina, 39, a Cuban immigrant, appeared to react to the lethal surges of electricity in a way similar to previously executed prisoners.

Slack said the malfunction at the Florida State Prison in the north Florida town of Starke sent a thick cloud of smoke through the execution chamber, prompting a security officer to open a window to let out the smoke.
"We do not have any idea at this point what happened to cause the flame," Slack said.

Medina, who spent 14 years on Florida's Death Row, was executed for the 1982 stabbing murder of an Orlando physical education teacher. The execution was carried out despite claims of mental illness by Medina, pleas for mercy from the victim's daughter, and a letter from the Pope John Paul II.
In a brief statement just before his execution Medina said: "I'm still innocent."
The electric chair used in Florida was built by prisoners in 1923. When an execution is carried out, the condemned prisoner is subjected to three cycles of electricity, peaking at 2,000 volts.

Tuesday's incident was the second time in nearly eight years that the chair has malfunctioned during an execution. On May 4, 1990, flames and smoke rose from the head of Jesse Tafero, who was convicted in 1976 of the murder of two police officers in Broward County.

Prison officials blamed the 1990 problem on a synthetic sponge that padded the headpiece worn during the execution. The sponge is soaked in saltwater to help conduct electricity and placed inside the helmet-like headpiece.

Medina was convicted in 1983 for the murder of Dorothy James, his neighbour and a 52-year-old public school teacher. He was arrested in north Florida driving James' Cadillac and the murder weapon was found in the car.
Medina came to the United States in 1980, a member of the Mariel boatlift that sent 110,000 Cubans to South Florida.
In January papal representative Archbishop Agostino Cacciavillan urged Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles to grant Medina clemency. But Chiles denied the request.
James' daughter, Lindi James, also requested repeatedly that Medina not be executed.
